claim: The multidrug transporter AcrB transports a broad range of drugs out of the cell by means of the proton-motive force.
source: The multidrug transporter AcrB transports a broad range of drugs out of the cell by means of the proton-motive force.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of AcrB, supported by established scientific knowledge about this transporter.

claim: The asymmetric crystal structure of trimeric AcrB suggests a functionally rotating mechanism for drug transport.
source: The asymmetric crystal structure of trimeric AcrB suggests a functionally rotating mechanism for drug transport.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous structural studies and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Protonation of Asp408 in the transmembrane portion of the drug-bound protomer drives the functional rotation.
source: Free energy calculations show that protonation of Asp408 in the transmembrane portion of the drug-bound protomer drives the functional rotation.
evidence: This claim is supported by free energy calculations performed in this study, representing computational data.

claim: Vertical shear motions among several transmembrane helices regulate alternate access of water in the transmembrane domain.
source: The conformational pathway identifies vertical shear motions among several transmembrane helices, which regulate alternate access of water in the transmembrane as well as peristaltic motions that pump drugs in the periplasm.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the conformational pathways obtained from simulations in this study.

claim: Vertical shear motions among several transmembrane helices regulate peristaltic motions that pump drugs in the periplasm.
source: The conformational pathway identifies vertical shear motions among several transmembrane helices, which regulate alternate access of water in the transmembrane as well as peristaltic motions that pump drugs in the periplasm.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the conformational pathways obtained from simulations in this study.

claim: Bacterial multidrug resistance (MDR) is an increasing threat to current antibiotic therapy.
source: Bacterial multidrug resistance (MDR) is an increasing threat to current antibiotic therapy (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2015.

claim: Resistance nodulation cell division (RND) transporters are one of the main causes of MDR in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Resistance nodulation cell division (RND) transporters are one of the main causes of MDR in Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of bacterial antibiotic resistance.

claim: RND transporters pump a wide spectrum of antibiotics out of the cell by means of proton- or sodium-motive forces.
source: These transporters pump a wide spectrum of antibiotics out of the cell by means of proton- or sodium-motive forces, conferring MDR to the bacterium when overexpressed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of RND transporters.

claim: In Escherichia coli, the AcrA-AcrB-TolC complex is largely responsible for MDR against many lipophilic antibiotics.
source: In Escherichia coli, the AcrA-AcrB-TolC complex is largely responsible for MDR against many lipophilic antibiotics (Du et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Du et al., 2015.

claim: The tripartite AcrA-AcrB-TolC assembly spans the periplasmic space between the inner and the outer membranes of the cell.
source: This tripartite assembly spans the periplasmic space between the inner and the outer membranes of the cell, transporting drugs from the cell to the medium.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about the AcrA-AcrB-TolC complex.

claim: TolC forms a generic outer membrane channel in which drugs can passively move towards the medium.
source: TolC, an outer membrane protein, forms a generic outer membrane channel in which drugs can passively move towards the medium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TolC function.

claim: AcrB is an inner membrane protein, primarily responsible for specificity towards drugs and their uptake, as well as for energy transduction.
source: AcrB is an inner membrane protein, primarily responsible for specificity towards drugs and their uptake, as well as for energy transduction.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AcrB function.

claim: AcrA acts as an adaptor that bridges TolC and AcrB.
source: AcrA acts as an adaptor that bridges TolC and AcrB (Du et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Du et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2017.

claim: AcrB is one of the best characterized RND transporters in both experiments and simulations.
source: AcrB is one of the best characterized RND transporters in both experiments and simulations, making it a prototype for studying the drug efflux mechanism of the RND family (Pos, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pos, 2009 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The structure of AcrB was first solved in a three-fold symmetric form.
source: The structure of AcrB was first solved in a three-fold symmetric form (Murakami et al., 2002), and later in an asymmetric form (Murakami et al., 2006; Seeger et al., 2006; Sennhauser et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The structure of AcrB was later solved in an asymmetric form.
source: The structure of AcrB was first solved in a three-fold symmetric form (Murakami et al., 2002), and later in an asymmetric form (Murakami et al., 2006; Seeger et al., 2006; Sennhauser et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: AcrB is a homotrimer with a triangular-prism shape.
source: AcrB is a homotrimer with a triangular-prism shape, and each protomer is made up of three domains (Figure 1A): the transmembrane (TM) domain and an extensive periplasmic portion comprising the porter and the funnel domains.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by crystal structures and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Each protomer of AcrB is made up of three domains: the transmembrane (TM) domain and an extensive periplasmic portion comprising the porter and the funnel domains.
source: AcrB is a homotrimer with a triangular-prism shape, and each protomer is made up of three domains (Figure 1A): the transmembrane (TM) domain and an extensive periplasmic portion comprising the porter and the funnel domains.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge supported by crystal structures and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The TM domain transfers protons across the inner membrane down the electrochemical gradient.
source: The TM domain transfers protons across the inner membrane down the electrochemical gradient (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the TM domain, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The porter domain is made of four subdomains, PN1, PN2, PC1 and PC2.
source: The porter domain is made of four subdomains, PN1, PN2, PC1 and PC2 (Figure 1B), and is responsible for drug transportation.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The porter domain is responsible for drug transportation.
source: The porter domain is made of four subdomains, PN1, PN2, PC1 and PC2 (Figure 1B), and is responsible for drug transportation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the porter domain.

claim: The funnel domain has a funnel-like shape with an exit pore that indirectly connects to TolC via AcrA.
source: The funnel domain has a funnel-like shape with an exit pore that indirectly connects to TolC via AcrA (Du et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Du et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2017.

claim: In the asymmetric structure, each protomer of AcrB adopts a distinct conformation that assumes one of the three functional states: Access, Binding, and Extrusion states.
source: In the asymmetric structure, each protomer of AcrB adopts a distinct conformation that assumes one of the three functional states in the drug transport cycle: Access (Murakami et al., 2006) (or Loose [Pos, 2009; Seeger et al., 2006]), Binding (Tight) and Extrusion (Open) states, or A, B and E, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The A state has entrances for drug uptake including an open cleft between PC1 and PC2, and a groove between TM helices, TM8 and TM9.
source: The A state has entrances (an open cleft between PC1 and PC2, and a groove between TM helices, TM8 and TM9) for drug uptake.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about the Access state.

claim: The B state has a binding pocket called the distal binding pocket formed by PN1, PN2 and PC1.
source: The B state has a binding pocket (called the distal binding pocket) formed by PN1, PN2 and PC1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The distal binding pocket contains many hydrophobic residues, as well as several charged and polar residues, contributing to broad substrate 'polyspecificity'.
source: This pocket contains many hydrophobic residues, as well as several charged and polar residues, contributing to broad substrate 'polyspecificity' (Takatsuka et al., 2010; Vargiu and Nikaido, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Takatsuka et al., 2010 and Vargiu and Nikaido, 2012.

claim: The E state has a drug exit pathway to the exit pore formed by an inclined central helix.
source: The E state has a drug exit pathway to the exit pore formed by an inclined central helix (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The tilt of the central helix is achieved by rigid body motions of a PC2/PN1 repeat.
source: The tilt of the central helix is achieved by rigid body motions of a PC2/PN1 repeat (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The rigid body motion of PC2/PN1 closes the PC1/PC2 cleft, leading to contraction of the binding pocket.
source: This motion also closes the PC1/PC2 cleft, leading to contraction of the binding pocket (Pos, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pos, 2009.

claim: The functional rotation mechanism is supported by biochemical studies.
source: This mechanism is supported by both biochemical studies (Seeger et al., 2008; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2007) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation studies (Schulz et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2010; Zuo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: The functional rotation mechanism is supported by molecular dynamics (MD) simulation studies.
source: This mechanism is supported by both biochemical studies (Seeger et al., 2008; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2007) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation studies (Schulz et al., 2010; Yao et al., 2010; Zuo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to MD simulation studies.

claim: The A state corresponds to an inward-facing state in the alternate access model.
source: The three functional states satisfy the conditions required in the alternate access model (Jardetzky, 1966): the A state (and possibly also the B state) corresponds to an inward-facing state, the E state represents an outward-facing state, and the B state is an occluded state.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with the alternate access model and supported by citation to Jardetzky, 1966.

claim: The B state possibly corresponds to an inward-facing state in the alternate access model.
source: The three functional states satisfy the conditions required in the alternate access model (Jardetzky, 1966): the A state (and possibly also the B state) corresponds to an inward-facing state, the E state represents an outward-facing state, and the B state is an occluded state.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparison with the alternate access model.

claim: The E state represents an outward-facing state in the alternate access model.
source: The three functional states satisfy the conditions required in the alternate access model (Jardetzky, 1966): the A state (and possibly also the B state) corresponds to an inward-facing state, the E state represents an outward-facing state, and the B state is an occluded state.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with the alternate access model and supported by citation to Jardetzky, 1966.

claim: The B state is an occluded state in the alternate access model.
source: The three functional states satisfy the conditions required in the alternate access model (Jardetzky, 1966): the A state (and possibly also the B state) corresponds to an inward-facing state, the E state represents an outward-facing state, and the B state is an occluded state.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with the alternate access model and supported by citation to Jardetzky, 1966.

claim: The TM domain of each protomer contains twelve α-helices (TM1–12).
source: The TM domain of each protomer contains twelve α-helices (TM1–12, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Essential residues for proton translocation are D407 and D408 on TM4, K940 on TM10, and T978 on TM11.
source: Essential residues for proton translocation are in the middle of the TM helices, D407 and D408 on TM4, K940 on TM10, and T978 on TM11.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on mutagenesis studies.

claim: AcrB mutants in which D407, D408, K940, or T978 are substituted by alanine are inactive.
source: AcrB mutants in which these residues are substituted by alanine are inactive (Guan and Nakae, 2001; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to mutagenesis studies.

claim: In the asymmetric structure, K940 shows a distinct side chain orientation in the E state compared with that in the A and B states.
source: In the asymmetric structure, K940 shows a distinct side chain orientation in the E state compared with that in the A and B states (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 1D.

claim: K940 tilts away from D408 and towards D407 and T978 in the E state.
source: Specifically, K940 tilts away from D408 and towards D407 and T978 in the E state, suggesting that transient protonation of D408 contributes to the TM conformational change.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: Transient protonation of D408 contributes to the TM conformational change.
source: Specifically, K940 tilts away from D408 and towards D407 and T978 in the E state, suggesting that transient protonation of D408 contributes to the TM conformational change.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: All-atom MD simulation by Yamane et al. (2013) showed that the protonation of D408 stabilized the E state.
source: Recently, all-atom MD simulation by Yamane et al. (2013) showed that the protonation of D408 stabilized the E state, whereas deprotonated D408 induced the conformation change of the TM domain toward the A state.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yamane et al., 2013.

claim: Deprotonated D408 induced the conformation change of the TM domain toward the A state.
source: Recently, all-atom MD simulation by Yamane et al. (2013) showed that the protonation of D408 stabilized the E state, whereas deprotonated D408 induced the conformation change of the TM domain toward the A state.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yamane et al., 2013.

claim: Eicher et al., (2014) showed by X-ray crystallography of AcrB mutants combined with MD simulations that conformational changes in the TM domain were related to the alternate access of water.
source: Eicher et al., (2014) showed, by X-ray crystallography of AcrB mutants combined with MD simulations, that these conformational changes in the TM domain were related to the alternate access of water, and in turn to the functional rotation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eicher et al., 2014.

claim: Conformational changes in the TM domain are related to the functional rotation.
source: Eicher et al., (2014) showed, by X-ray crystallography of AcrB mutants combined with MD simulations, that these conformational changes in the TM domain were related to the alternate access of water, and in turn to the functional rotation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eicher et al., 2014.

claim: The simulation system comprised 480,074 atoms.
source: Using an explicit solvent/lipid all-atom model (480,074 atoms), we identified conformational transition pathways in one step of the functional rotation for the complete AcrB trimers with different protonation states.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation system used in this study.

claim: System 1 has an energy minimum close to the initial BEA state (at image 5).
source: While system 1 has an energy minimum close to the initial BEA state (at image 5), the minimum of system 2 is shifted towards the final EAB state (at image 15), indicating that the protonation state in system 2 drives the functional rotation.
evidence: This is based on free energy calculations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The minimum of system 2 is shifted towards the final EAB state (at image 15).
source: While system 1 has an energy minimum close to the initial BEA state (at image 5), the minimum of system 2 is shifted towards the final EAB state (at image 15), indicating that the protonation state in system 2 drives the functional rotation.
evidence: This is based on free energy calculations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The protonation state in system 2 drives the functional rotation.
source: While system 1 has an energy minimum close to the initial BEA state (at image 5), the minimum of system 2 is shifted towards the final EAB state (at image 15), indicating that the protonation state in system 2 drives the functional rotation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the free energy calculations comparing systems 1 and 2.

claim: The release of the drug is the main factor for the increase in free energy in the late stage (images 20–30) of system 2.
source: This relation suggests that the release of the drug is the main factor for the increase in free energy in the late stage (images 20–30) of system 2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the free energy profile and drug binding free energy calculations.

claim: Previous simulation studies suggested that asymmetric trimeric states are unstable without a bound drug.
source: Previous simulation studies (Yamane et al., 2013; Yao et al., 2010) suggested that asymmetric trimeric states are unstable without a bound drug, while the symmetric AAA state becomes most stable, avoiding the rebinding of the released drug.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous simulation studies.

claim: The symmetric AAA state becomes most stable without a bound drug.
source: Previous simulation studies (Yamane et al., 2013; Yao et al., 2010) suggested that asymmetric trimeric states are unstable without a bound drug, while the symmetric AAA state becomes most stable, avoiding the rebinding of the released drug.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous simulation studies.

claim: The protonation at D408 in protomer I destabilizes the TM domain because of a strong positive electrostatic potential bias.
source: Electrostatic potential energy maps before and after the transformation of the protonation state reveal that the TM domain of protomer I is destabilized by the protonation because of a strong positive electrostatic potential bias (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on electrostatic potential calculations shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The positive electrostatic potential bias is caused by the surrounding positively charged residues R971 and K940.
source: This bias is caused by the surrounding positively charged residues R971 and K940, whose side-chains orient towards D408p.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and electrostatic analysis.

claim: The side-chain of R971 reorients downwards (towards the cytoplasm) at image 15 of system 2.
source: The side-chain of R971 (on TM11) reorients downwards (towards the cytoplasm), as does D408p (on TM4) due to repulsion from K940 (on TM10).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the conformational pathway shown in Figure 3C.

claim: D408p reorients downwards due to repulsion from K940.
source: The side-chain of R971 (on TM11) reorients downwards (towards the cytoplasm), as does D408p (on TM4) due to repulsion from K940 (on TM10).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claim: The downshift motions involve TM4 and TM11, whereas TM10 remains at the original position.
source: These motions involve the downshift of TM4 and TM11, whereas TM10 remains at the original position.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the conformational pathway.

claim: Downshifts occur in TM3, TM4, TM5, TM6, and TM11.
source: By monitoring the centers-of-mass for the other TM helices along the conformational pathway, we found that downshifts occur not only in TM4 and TM11 but also in TM3, TM5 and TM6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Eicher et al. (2014) recognized two rigid assemblies in the TM domain, R1 (TM1 and TM3 to TM6) and R2 (TM7 and TM9 to TM12).
source: Based on their analysis of crystal structures, Eicher et al. (2014) recognized two rigid assemblies in the TM domain, R1 (TM1 and TM3 to TM6) and R2 (TM7 and TM9 to TM12), which change their mutual arrangement during the transitions among B, E and A states.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eicher et al., 2014.

claim: R1 and R2 change their mutual arrangement during the transitions among B, E and A states.
source: Based on their analysis of crystal structures, Eicher et al. (2014) recognized two rigid assemblies in the TM domain, R1 (TM1 and TM3 to TM6) and R2 (TM7 and TM9 to TM12), which change their mutual arrangement during the transitions among B, E and A states.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eicher et al., 2014.

claim: The downshift motions of the TM helices can be interpreted as a vertical shear motion of R1 against R2.
source: In terms of R1/R2 rigid body motions, the downshift motions of the TM helices can be interpreted as a vertical shear motion of R1 against R2.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural analysis of the conformational pathway.

claim: TM11 in R2 moves downwards together with R1.
source: TM11 in R2 is the exception, because it moves downwards together with R1.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the conformational pathway.

claim: Previous structural studies mostly focused on lateral shear motions and rocking motions of R1 and R2.
source: Previous structural studies mostly focused on lateral shear motions and rocking motions (Du et al., 2015; Eicher et al., 2014) of R1 and R2, whereas our observations clarify that protonation mainly induces a vertical shear motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Protonation mainly induces a vertical shear motion.
source: Previous structural studies mostly focused on lateral shear motions and rocking motions (Du et al., 2015; Eicher et al., 2014) of R1 and R2, whereas our observations clarify that protonation mainly induces a vertical shear motion.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the conformational pathway in this study.

claim: Downshifts of specific TM helices, including TM11, can be discerned in the crystal structures when the TM helices of different states are properly aligned.
source: Indeed, downshifts of the specific TM helices, including TM11, can be discerned in the crystal structures when the TM helices of different states are properly aligned (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of crystal structures shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: At image 5 of system 1 with D408, a water wire channel is observed from periplasmic D924 to the conflux space.
source: At image 5 of system 1 with D408, a water wire channel is clearly observed from periplasmic D924 (a possible transient proton binding site to facilitate proton uptake on TM10 [Eicher et al., 2014]) to the space in the middle of the helices (called the conflux space [Fischer and Kandt, 2011]) surrounded by hydrophobic residues (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on water distribution analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: D924 is a possible transient proton binding site to facilitate proton uptake on TM10.
source: At image 5 of system 1 with D408, a water wire channel is clearly observed from periplasmic D924 (a possible transient proton binding site to facilitate proton uptake on TM10 [Eicher et al., 2014]) to the space in the middle of the helices (called the conflux space [Fischer and Kandt, 2011]) surrounded by hydrophobic residues (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eicher et al., 2014.

claim: A minor water pathway comes from E346 which merges into the conflux space.
source: Also, a minor water pathway comes from E346 (another possible transient proton-binding site on TM2), which merges into the conflux space.
evidence: This is based on water distribution analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: E346 is another possible transient proton-binding site on TM2.
source: Also, a minor water pathway comes from E346 (another possible transient proton-binding site on TM2), which merges into the conflux space.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of a water pathway.

claim: At the cytoplasmic end, the side chain of R971 breaks the channel, preventing the leakage of protons.
source: At the cytoplasmic end, the side chain of R971 breaks the channel, preventing the leakage of protons (Eicher et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eicher et al., 2014 and water distribution analysis.

claim: At image 15 of system 2 with D408p, there is no water channel coming from the periplasm.
source: By contrast, water distribution at image 15 of system 2 with D408p is completely different due to the vertical shear motion in the TM domain (Figure 3E). There is no water channel coming from the periplasm, resulting from the collapse of the conflux space by the downshifts of TM4 and TM11; distances between residue pairs L400–T933 and L937–F982 decrease, preventing water molecules from entering the conflux space (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on water distribution analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The collapse of the conflux space results from the downshifts of TM4 and TM11.
source: There is no water channel coming from the periplasm, resulting from the collapse of the conflux space by the downshifts of TM4 and TM11; distances between residue pairs L400–T933 and L937–F982 decrease, preventing water molecules from entering the conflux space (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on structural and water distribution analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: At image 15 of system 2, the side chain of R971 opens towards cytoplasmic bulk water, exposing the protonation site and providing a possible proton release pathway.
source: On the other hand, the side chain of R971 opens towards cytoplasmic bulk water, exposing the protonation site and providing a possible proton release pathway.
evidence: This is based on structural and water distribution analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: R971 is an electrostatic gate for proton diffusion to the cytoplasm.
source: Thus, R971 is an electrostatic gate for proton diffusion to the cytoplasm, analogous to the selectivity filter of aquaporins as discussed in previous studies (Eicher et al., 2014; Eriksson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Image 5 of system 1 and image 15 of system 2 exemplify the alternate access of water that occurs concurrently with the proton translocation.
source: In summary, these two states, image 5 of system 1 and image 15 of system 2, exemplify the alternate access of water that occurs concurrently with the proton translocation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the water distribution analysis.

claim: The string method yielded synchronized pathways for system 2, but not for system 1.
source: Remarkably, however, the string method yielded synchronized pathways for system 2, but not for system 1. This suggests the existence of a coupling between the remote sites (the porter and TM domains) in system 2.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the conformational pathways shown in Figure 4.

claim: There is a coupling between the remote sites (the porter and TM domains) in system 2.
source: Remarkably, however, the string method yielded synchronized pathways for system 2, but not for system 1. This suggests the existence of a coupling between the remote sites (the porter and TM domains) in system 2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synchronized pathways observed in system 2.

claim: System 2 exhibits larger correlations between the TM helices and the porter domain than does system 1.
source: Clearly, system 2 (broken lines in the figure) exhibits larger correlations than does system 1 (solid lines).
evidence: This is based on mutual information analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Protomer I shows the greatest correlation between the TM domain and the porter domain among the three protomers.
source: Protomer I, among the three protomers, shows the greatest correlation, indicating that the TM domain motion of protomer I that is induced by proton translocation is harnessed for the rearrangement of the porter domain.
evidence: This is based on mutual information analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The TM domain motion of protomer I that is induced by proton translocation is harnessed for the rearrangement of the porter domain.
source: Protomer I, among the three protomers, shows the greatest correlation, indicating that the TM domain motion of protomer I that is induced by proton translocation is harnessed for the rearrangement of the porter domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutual information analysis.

claim: The transition from the B to the E state is the energy-consuming step.
source: This means that the transition from the B to the E state is the energy-consuming step (Pos, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis and supported by citation to Pos, 2009.

claim: In protomer I (B→E), high correlations were observed between TM4–TM6, TM8 and TM11, and PN1 and PC2.
source: In protomer I (B→E), high correlations were observed between TM4–TM6, TM8 and TM11, and PN1 and PC2 (and also weakly with PN2).
evidence: This is based on mutual information analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The coil-to-helix transition of TM8 is sterically hindered by the sidechain of F459 on TM5 in the B state.
source: In particular, the coil-to-helix transition of TM8, which leverages the rigid body motion in PN1/PC2 (see Figure 1B and Figure 5), is sterically hindered by the sidechain of F459 on TM5 in the B state (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Downshift of TM5 causes the F459 sidechain to flip, allowing the coil-to-helix transition of TM8.
source: Downshift of TM5 causes the F459 sidechain to flip, allowing the coil-to-helix transition of TM8.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The downshift of TM5 reduces the barrier for the extension of TM8, expediting the PN1/PC2 rigid body motion to open the exit gate for the drug.
source: Thus, the downshift of TM5 reduces the barrier for the extension of TM8, expediting the PN1/PC2 rigid body motion to open the exit gate for the drug.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis of the coupling mechanism.

claim: Protomer I exhibits weak linkage between PN2 and several TM helices.
source: Protomer I also exhibits weak linkage between PN2 and several TM helices.
evidence: This is based on mutual information analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The downshift of the TM helices decreases contacts between the TM domain and PN2.
source: The downshift of the TM helices decreases contacts between the TM domain and PN2, and may accommodate the rearrangement of PN2.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: Previous studies indicated that a slight tilting of TM2 is coupled to PN2 motion.
source: Previous studies indicated that a slight tilting of TM2 is coupled to PN2 motion (Du et al., 2015; Eicher et al., 2014), which is also observed here as weak correlations between TM2 and PN2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and observed in this study.

claim: Protomer II (E→A) has only a local correlation network between TM5 and TM8 and PN1 and PC2.
source: Unlike protomer I, protomer II (E→A) has only a local correlation network between TM5 and TM8 (and weakly with TM10) and PN1 and PC2.
evidence: This is based on mutual information analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The relatively weak correlation in protomer II is associated with the reverse helix-to-coil transition of TM8, which closes the drug exit gate.
source: This relatively weak correlation is associated with the reverse helix-to-coil transition of TM8, which closes the drug exit gate.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and correlation analysis.

claim: Yamane et al. (2013) described a scenario for the E→A transition involving twisting motions of TM4 and TM10 interfering with TM1, PN1, and PN2.
source: Also, weak correlations can be seen in TM1, TM4, and TM10, which are consistent with the scenario described by Yamane et al. (2013) for the E→A transition: twisting motions of TM4 and TM10 interfere with TM1, PN1, and PN2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yamane et al., 2013.

claim: Protomer III (A→B) has rather weak correlations between PN2 and the TM helices.
source: Protomer III (A→B) has rather weak correlations between PN2 and the TM helices, which may be related to the rearrangement of PN2/PC1 on distal binding pocket formation and the influence of rising TM helices on contact with the PN2 domain.
evidence: This is based on mutual information analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The local and weak correlations in protomers II and III suggest that the minor coupling either occurs indirectly via interfacial interactions between protomers or is mediated by drug binding.
source: These local and weak correlations in protomers II and III suggest that the minor coupling either occurs indirectly via interfacial interactions between protomers or is mediated by drug binding, not being harnessed by proton translocation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the correlation analysis.

claim: Coupling of the TM and the porter domains during B→E is the energy-consuming process.
source: Coupling of the TM and the porter domains during B→E is the energy-consuming process.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the free energy and correlation analyses in this study.

claim: Protonation of D408 in the B state drives a vertical shear motion in the TM domain.
source: Protonation of D408 in the B state drives a vertical shear motion in the TM domain, which regulates the alternate access of water (the conflux space closes, R971 opens towards the cytoplasm) as well as the motion of the porter domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and energetic analyses in this study.

claim: TM8 works as a transmitter between the TM domain and the porter domain.
source: In this process, the TM8 works as a transmitter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and correlation analyses.

claim: The extension of TM8 induces the rigid body motion of the PN2/PC1 tandem, opening the drug exit gate and shrinking the distal binding pocket.
source: It's extension induces the rigid body motion of the PN2/PC1 tandem, opening the drug exit gate and shrinking the distal binding pocket.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the conformational pathway.

claim: In the E→A step, the porter domain of E relaxes towards A without systematic couplings with the TM domain.
source: In the E→A step, the porter domain of E relaxes towards A without systematic couplings with the TM domain, perhaps driven mainly by cooperativity (interfacial interactions) between protomers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation analysis showing weak correlations in protomer II.

claim: Cross-linking experiments suggested that steric clashes occur between the E protomers.
source: Cross-linking experiments (Seeger et al., 2008; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2007) and coarse-grained model simulations (Yao et al., 2010) suggested that steric clashes occur between the E protomers, making two or more E-state protomers in the trimer energetically unfavorable, and making the E→A transition occur spontaneously.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to cross-linking experiments.

claim: Coarse-grained model simulations suggested that steric clashes occur between the E protomers.
source: Cross-linking experiments (Seeger et al., 2008; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2007) and coarse-grained model simulations (Yao et al., 2010) suggested that steric clashes occur between the E protomers, making two or more E-state protomers in the trimer energetically unfavorable, and making the E→A transition occur spontaneously.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to coarse-grained model simulations.

claim: Two or more E-state protomers in the trimer are energetically unfavorable.
source: Cross-linking experiments (Seeger et al., 2008; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2007) and coarse-grained model simulations (Yao et al., 2010) suggested that steric clashes occur between the E protomers, making two or more E-state protomers in the trimer energetically unfavorable, and making the E→A transition occur spontaneously.
evidence: This is an inference based on the steric clashes between E protomers.

claim: The E→A transition occurs spontaneously.
source: Cross-linking experiments (Seeger et al., 2008; Takatsuka and Nikaido, 2007) and coarse-grained model simulations (Yao et al., 2010) suggested that steric clashes occur between the E protomers, making two or more E-state protomers in the trimer energetically unfavorable, and making the E→A transition occur spontaneously.
evidence: This is an inference based on the energetic unfavorability of multiple E-state protomers.

claim: In the A→B step, drug that is bound in A may 'catalyze' formation of the distal binding pocket in the PN2/PC1 tandem.
source: In the A→B step, drug that is bound in A may 'catalyze' (Moradi et al., 2015) formation of the distal binding pocket in the PN2/PC1 tandem.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Moradi et al., 2015.

claim: The conformational change in the A→B step increases the number of contacts with the TM domain and drives the TM helices upwards.
source: The resulting conformational change increases the number of contacts with the TM domain and drives the TM helices upwards.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural analysis.

claim: The present study provides evidence that energy is consumed to release the drug (i.e., the B-to-E step).
source: The present study provides evidence that energy is consumed to release the drug (i.e., the B-to-E step).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the free energy calculations in this study.

claim: Pos's model predicted that energy is consumed in the B-to-E step in analogy to F0F1-ATP synthase.
source: This energy consumption was predicted by Pos's model in analogy to F0F1-ATP synthase, where the energy is used to release the ATP from the beta-subunit.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pos's model and the analogy to F0F1-ATP synthase.

claim: This study provides a simple molecular mechanism for energy transduction from the TM domain to the porter domain in terms of the vertical shear motion in the TM domain.
source: This study also provides a simple molecular mechanism for energy transduction from the TM domain to the porter domain in terms of the vertical shear motion in the TM domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and energetic analyses in this study.

claim: The same type of vertical shear motions can be seen in other transporters that employ the so-called elevator alternating-access mechanism.
source: The same type of vertical shear motions can be seen in other transporters that employ the so-called elevator alternating-access mechanism (Drew and Boudker, 2016; Slotboom, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on other transporters.

claim: Computational work by Eicher et al. (2014) indicated that not only D408 but also D407 is protonated in the E state.
source: The computational work by Eicher et al. (2014) indicated that not only D408 but also D407 is protonated in the E state, suggesting a stoichiometry of two protons per one substrate.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eicher et al., 2014.

claim: pKa calculations by Yamane et al. (2013) showed that only D408 should be protonated in the E state.
source: On the other hand, pKa calculations by Yamane et al. (2013) showed that only D408 should be protonated in the E state.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yamane et al., 2013.

claim: MD simulations by Yamane et al. (2013) showed that the protonation of both D407 and D408 destabilizes the structure of the TM domain.
source: Furthermore, their MD simulations showed that the protonation of both D407 and D408 destabilizes the structure of the TM domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yamane et al., 2013.

claim: The impact of transient deprotonation/protonation of D408 is enough to drive functional rotation and the extrusion of a drug.
source: The consistency of two independent calculations has confirmed that the impact of transient deprotonation/protonation of D408 is certainly enough to drive functional rotation and the extrusion of a drug.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the consistency of free energy calculations in this study.

claim: The crystal structure of the asymmetric AcrB trimer (PDB entry: 4DX5) with bound minocycline in the distal binding pocket of protomer I was used for MD simulations.
source: The crystal structure of the asymmetric AcrB trimer (PDB entry: 4DX5 [Eicher et al., 2012]) with bound minocycline in the distal binding pocket of protomer I (B state) was used for MD simulations.
evidence: This describes the starting structure for the simulations.

claim: The AcrB trimer was embedded in an equilibrated lipid bilayer membrane of POPE.
source: The AcrB trimer was embedded in an equilibrated lipid bilayer membrane of POPE (1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine).
evidence: This describes the simulation system setup.

claim: Twelve POPE molecules were manually packed into the hole in the TM center of AcrB.
source: Twelve POPE molecules were manually packed into the hole (six for the upper leaflet and six for the lower leaflet).
evidence: This describes the simulation system setup.

claim: D408 of protomer II was protonated for system 1.
source: D408 of protomer II (E state) was protonated for system 1 while D408 of protomer I (B state) was protonated for system 2.
evidence: This describes the protonation state setup for the simulations.

claim: D408 of protomer I was protonated for system 2.
source: D408 of protomer II (E state) was protonated for system 1 while D408 of protomer I (B state) was protonated for system 2.
evidence: This describes the protonation state setup for the simulations.

source: The final system comprised 480,074 atoms.
